name: Jiawei Xiaoyao pill (Chinese herbal formula; kamishoyosan in Japan)
short: Japanese form (kamishoyosan), case reports: respiratory distress (ARDS), liver injury; colon-vein disease (mesenteric phlebosclerosis), mostly long-term. Oral pill trials: no significant difference.
text: Jiawei Xiaoyao is a Chinese herbal formula taken by mouth; a laboratory abstract gives Jiaweixiaoyao-san as its Chinese name, Kamishoyo-san as its Japanese name and Gamisoyo-san as its Korean name, and a second gives Kami-shoyo-san as the Kampo name of Jia-Wei-Xiao-Yao-San. Neither pill trial abstract lists the pill's herbs, so the link between the pill and the Japanese and Korean preparations rests on the shared formula name. A laboratory analysis measured geniposide in Jiawei Xiaoyao pills, and an abstract on mesenteric phlebosclerosis describes geniposide as a major constituent of gardenia fruits; a Japanese study lists the Japanese preparation's 10 herbs as including Bupleurum, peony, Angelica sinensis and licorice (Glycyrrhiza) roots. A 2022 review of the adverse effects of Kampo medicines in general (not of this formula) lists pseudoaldosteronism caused by licorice among the known adverse effects linked to overdose of Kampo formulas, and says mesenteric phlebosclerosis caused by long-term use of gardenia fruit has been reported; PubMed searches found no report of pseudoaldosteronism naming this formula. The most serious harms found were reported with the Japanese preparation (kamishoyosan), mostly after long-term use, in case reports and case series, which show associations rather than proof. Mesenteric phlebosclerosis, a rare disease in which the wall of the right colon thickens and its veins calcify: in a summary of 25 patients with the disease, 12 had taken kamisyoyosan (as spelled in that abstract) for a mean of 12.8 years, and the one ingredient common to all 25 patients' herbal medicines was gardenia fruit (sansisi), whose constituent geniposide the authors associate with the disease when used long term; a study of 42 patients with the disease reported that about 90% of the patients the authors treated had taken Chinese herbal medicine, particularly kamishoyosan, orengedokuto and gardenia fruit, and that symptoms worsened in patients who kept taking the medicine after onset; and a case report, whose title links the disease to Kampo medicines containing gardenia fruit taken by mouth, describes a woman in her 50s who had taken kamishoyosan for 13 years, whose colon lesions spread over time; in her colon biopsies, collagen deposits around the vessels were already present when the total amount of gardenia fruit (Sanshishi) she had taken was low. Severity (data on the disease in general, not on this formula): a 2021 case report and systematic review of 240 published cases of the disease, mainly from East Asia, found that 78.7% of the patients had taken herbal medicines, and that 41.6% had severe symptoms and had surgery while 58.4% recovered with conservative (non-surgical) treatment; the abstract does not say how many patients these last two figures are based on, and its comparison of lesion sites counts 82 patients treated surgically and 115 treated conservatively, not all 240. A 2017 case report describes colon cancer found together with the disease in a 63-year-old woman who had taken a Chinese herb containing gardenia fruit for over 18 years; its literature review found 10 reported cases of colorectal cancer together with the disease, 5 of them associated with a Chinese herb containing gardenia fruit, and the authors speculate that genipin, a metabolite of gardenia fruit, may be linked to cancer of the right side of the colon. That abstract does not name this formula, and the link to cancer is the authors' speculation. Lung: a case report describes adult respiratory distress syndrome in a 59-year-old woman given Kamisyoyo-san (as spelled) for seborrhoeic dermatitis, with a positive lymphocyte stimulation test for the formula. Liver: a title-only record reports liver injury induced by kamishoyosan, and a 2014 review of herbal liver toxicity lists Jia Wei Xia Yao San (as spelled) and Kamishoyosan among products for which case reports or case series since 2011 provided evidence of liver toxicity, without giving numbers or severity. In trials of the pill itself: in a placebo-controlled trial in 144 women with premenstrual syndrome over 3 menstrual cycles, adverse events, severe adverse events, withdrawals due to adverse events and adverse reactions did not differ significantly between groups, with no clinically significant adverse medical events related to the pill; in a 4-week placebo-controlled trial in 144 adults with functional dyspepsia, with blood counts, liver and kidney tests and an electrocardiogram among the safety checks, there were 30 adverse events with the pill and 20 with placebo (P = 0.240), and the abstract does not say what they were. In a randomized double-blind trial in 210 outpatients with mild to moderate depression and anxiety, Jiawei Xiaoyao capsules (another form of the Chinese formula) were compared with the antidepressant sertraline for 8 weeks, and the rate of adverse events was the same in the two groups. In a randomized pilot trial in postmenopausal women, Jia-Wey Shiau-Yau San (as spelled) had a relatively lower rate of stopping because of adverse effects than continuous combined hormone replacement therapy, in particular for bleeding and breast tenderness. In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of kamishoyosan in 205 women with menopausal symptoms, no serious adverse effect was reported; in a second double-blind placebo-controlled trial in women with climacteric disorder (20 per arm, randomized after a placebo run-in among women who had not responded to placebo), adverse drug reactions and adverse events did not differ between the arms and no serious events were reported; and in an open-label randomized trial that enrolled 50 patients with premenstrual syndrome (the abstract does not say how many took kamishoyosan), the only adverse event related to kamishoyosan was headache in one patient. Interactions: in an open-label crossover study of 18 people taking the antidepressant escitalopram, in which one of two groups also took Gami-soyosan (the Korean preparation) for 7 days, escitalopram exposure rose only slightly with each herbal medicine and the authors found no significant effect on escitalopram levels (16 of the 18 completed the study); in laboratory tests, Gamisoyo-san inhibited the drug-metabolising enzymes CYP1A2, CYP2C19 and UGT1A1, and kamishoyosan inhibited CYP3A4, with those authors suggesting that excessive doses of kamishoyosan might cause interactions with medicines broken down by CYP3A4; these are laboratory findings, not observations in people.
